findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Scope fail-closed to the trust-list key: treat the list as 'set' (and fail closed) only when `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` / `REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS` is present but fails to coerce; keep an unrelated config error from turning a list-unset environment into `untrusted`, and add a test for a list-unset environment with an unrelated malformed key.

ADR 0125 §3 says fail closed when 'a list that cannot be read or parsed'. That is scoped to the list, not to the whole configuration.
findings.finding: The fail-closed rule is scoped to any failure to read or compose configuration, not to the trust-list key itself. In an environment that never set `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` but has an unrelated malformed config key, every op-cert would become `untrusted`. That contradicts 'List unset: unchanged in this story' (AC2) and reverses the existing policy in `_required_environment` that 'Unreadable config cannot enable a restriction'.
findings.location: Approach step 2 ('If the list cannot be read or coerced, the helper fails closed (`untrusted` …), never "unset"'); AC2
scenarios: A developer clone or CI runner with no trust list has a typo in an unrelated `rebar.toml` or user-config key. Every plan-review and completion certificate verifies `untrusted`, and claim and close gates block, with a reason about an unrelated key.
A transient compose failure in the MCP or CLI flips all op-certs to `untrusted` in a deployment that has no list.
findings.suggested_fix: In the trust-list helper, catch ConfigError and fail closed only when the error names `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` or the raw env var/TOML layer actually sets that key. Otherwise keep the list-unset path, matching `_required_environment`'s 'unreadable config cannot enable a restriction' rule. Add a test: list unset plus a malformed unrelated key, where a pinned or embedded-key certificate still verifies as before.

src/rebar/_opcert_verify.py:338-340: "A configured trust list replaces every other trust root" (pinned keys are skipped when any list is set).

docs/adr/0125-opcert-trust-per-environment.md:70-72: "The list lives in the verifying environment's own configuration … and the repository's own `rebar.toml` does not set it"; line 95-96: the gate's environment is one "which the change under test cannot edit".
No existing project-layer guard for config keys was found (search of src/rebar for a project-layer restriction returned only provenance and mapping helpers).
findings.finding: The plan registers `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` as an ordinary config key, so it resolves through every layer, including the repo-committed project layer (`rebar.toml` / `pyproject.toml [tool.rebar]`). Once set, the list replaces every other trust root, pinned keys included. A change under review (a lower-trust actor relative to the verifier) can therefore commit a `[verify] trusted_opcert_keys` entry pairing an environment id with its own key. Any verifier that does not set the list through env, user config or CLI (CI, the review bot, a merge gate with `require_environment` set but no list in its env) would then certify the attacker's op-certs as `trust_list`. This contradicts ADR 0125, which says the repository's `rebar.toml` does not set the list.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (config key registration in `_SECTIONS["verify"]`) and step 2 (`verify_opcert_record` trust root)
scenarios: A Gerrit change adds `[verify] trusted_opcert_keys = ["<required-env-id> ssh-ed25519 <attacker-key>"]` to `rebar.toml`. A CI or merge-gate job running `verify_opcert_record` on that checkout with `require_environment` in its env but no list in its env then certifies the attacker-signed op-cert as `trust_list` and skips the pinned-key check that would otherwise apply.
The plan-review attest gate or `rebar validate`, run on a contributor's branch, reads the branch's own committed list and reports its self-signed certificates as `certified`.
findings.suggested_fix: In step 1, state that `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` is honoured only from the user, env and CLI layers. One way is to check in `_ordered_layers`/`coerce_sparse` that raises `ConfigError` (naming ADR 0125) when the key appears in the `project` layer. Add a case to `tests/unit/test_opcert_trust_list.py` that writes the key into a store-root `rebar.toml` and asserts it is rejected and never yields `trust_list`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the disposition of a malformed or empty trust-list value per arm: whether config load raises fatally or verification alone fails closed (permanent until redeploy), and what `/health` `opcert` reports (`error` set, never a pin-file fallback).
evidence: Step 1: "requires `<env_id> <key-type> <base64> [comment]` with decodable base64, else `ConfigError` naming the entry position"
Step 1: "`(\"verify\", \"trusted_opcert_keys\")` joins `_EMPTY_ENV_FAULT_KEYS` so an empty `${VAR}` raises"
Step 2: "If the list cannot be read or coerced, the helper fails closed (`untrusted`, reason names the config error), never \"unset\""
Step 4 is silent on the malformed-list case, while the live AC expects "no `error`"
findings.finding: The plan states two different dispositions for a malformed or empty trust-list value. Step 1 has the coercer raise `ConfigError`, and an empty `${VAR}` joins `_EMPTY_ENV_FAULT_KEYS`; if config loading is eager, that error is fatal to every command and to MCP startup. Step 2 says the verify helper "fails closed (`untrusted`, reason names the config error)", which confines the failure to verification. The plan does not say which arm the deployed MCP server hits. It also does not say what the health probe (Step 4) reports when the list cannot be read: `error`, degraded, or a fallback to the pin file.
scenarios: A typo in `REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS` in compose either crashes the rebar-mcp container on startup (fatal, blue-green roll fails) or leaves it up reporting every op-cert `untrusted`. Operators cannot predict which.
With a malformed list, health could fall back to `trust_source: pin_file` and report healthy while verification fails closed.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a sentence to steps 2 and 4: a malformed or empty list is a permanent configuration fault. `verify_opcert_record` returns `untrusted` naming the `ConfigError`. `opcert_signing_status` reports `expected: true`, `matched: false`, `trust_source: "trust_list"` with `error` set, and never falls back to the pin file. Add a health test for this case.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Name the owner and procedure for changing the deployed trust list on key rotation (both infra files updated together, parity test as the guard), and state when the pre-rotation `nava-opcert-prod` key is removed from the list.
evidence: "identical values listing the 3 keys now pinned: env `9f1c8e42-...` with `nava-opcert-prod` and `nava-opcert-prod rotated-20260907`"
"`REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS` in the `mcp` environment of `infra/compose/docker-compose.yml` and as `-e` in `mcp_run_new` of `infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh`"
No statement of who updates the list on rotation or when an old key is removed
findings.finding: The trust list is shared, security-critical state whose update and retirement lifecycle is unstated. The value is duplicated verbatim in two infra files, with parity enforced only by a test. During the interim a third copy lives in the pin file, and nothing checks the list against it. No owner or procedure is named for adding a newly rotated key or removing a superseded one. The pre-rotation `nava-opcert-prod` key is deployed as trusted alongside `rotated-20260907` with no stated retirement condition, so a superseded and possibly compromised key stays trusted indefinitely.
scenarios: The next op-cert rotation updates the pin file or one infra file but not the other, and verification diverges until someone notices.
The pre-rotation nava key is never removed, so records it signs after rotation still verify as `certified`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State in the plan that setting the list switches the MCP from advisory envelope_key trust to enforcing (per ADR 0125), and add a pre-rollout step or AC that lists open tickets whose current op-certs were signed by keys outside the 3-key list, so that intended `untrusted` outcomes are known and re-certified before the container rolls.
evidence: Plan: 'Rebar's MCP server must never run without its list; today it trusts via `_opcert_trust_root`… So the list and its deployment land BEFORE the sibling story.'

src/rebar/_opcert_verify.py `_opcert_trust_root`: with no require_environment set, it falls back to the embedded key ('envelope_key'), so today the MCP certifies valid certificates from any environment.
docs/manifest-signing.md: 'Certification environment is **not** a gate under current operator policy … A certificate minted by another environment therefore certifies here.'

ADR 0125 Consequences: 'On the MCP server, a certificate signed in another environment … reads as `untrusted`, so claims and closes through the server need certificates the server's listed keys signed.' The plan does not carry this consequence or any rollout handling.
src/rebar/llm/plan_review/attest_gate.py `plan_review_status` wraps `claim_gate_check`, which uses `signing.verify_signature`, so `untrusted` blocks claims through the MCP.
findings.finding: The plan presents the deployment as preserving current behaviour ('must never run without its list'). In practice, setting the list switches the live MCP server from advisory (embedded-key `envelope_key` certification of any environment's valid certificate) to enforcing. On rollout, existing and in-flight certificates signed by unlisted environments become `untrusted` at the MCP claim gate (`claim_gate_check` / `plan_review_status`) and at close. The plan does not state this consequence, does not check the live tickets store for affected certificates, and its live AC checks only `/health`.
findings.location: Context / Problem; Approach step 5 (Deployment); AC 'live MCP /health'
scenarios: A ticket reviewed through a local `review-plan` in an unlisted developer environment is claimed or closed through the MCP right after autodeploy rolls. It is now refused as `untrusted`, although it certified a minute earlier.
An operator reads the green `/health` AC as proof the rollout is safe while claims start failing.

Approach step 2: 'If the list cannot be read or coerced, the helper fails closed (untrusted…)'. A bad deployed value would therefore quietly reject every certificate, not crash the container.
findings.finding: The plan has no way to catch, and no rollback path for, a deployed trust list that doesn't match the real signing keys. Autodeploy's blue-green cutover never looks at the opcert trust state. The only check is a one-time manual SSM curl of /health after rollout, and the plan doesn't say what the operator does if it shows `matched: false` or an `error`. Meanwhile every certified op-cert verification on the live MCP would fail closed as `untrusted`.
findings.location: Approach step 5 / AC '[non-codebase] After autodeploy rolls this change, the live MCP /health opcert field reads expected: true, matched: true…'
scenarios: A typo or bad base64 in the committed literal passes the parity test (both copies share the typo) but fails coercion at runtime. The container becomes healthy, cuts over, and then rejects every op-cert as `untrusted` until someone runs the manual curl.
